title: 7. Personal Assistants
section: From a Tool to a Teammate
text:
From a Tool to a Teammate


A research team

Many agents, different roles, working together
They propose, attack, verify, and re-check each other



A personal assistant

One agent that carries work across sessions
Remembers context, uses your tools, acts on your behalf




Two shapes where agents pay off: a panel that pressure-tests ideas and data, and an assistant that just gets recurring things done.

title: 7. Personal Assistants
text:
Not the Same as Day 6


Day 6 — Student Projects

Agents students build as the deliverable
The product is the point; the learning is the design and the verification



Today — Your Assistants

Agents that work for you, on your research and your tasks
The product is your output; the agent is the labor




Same underlying idea — an agent that decides and acts — pointed two ways: something students make, versus something that makes your week lighter.

title: 7. Personal Assistants
text: A Research Team

title: 7. Personal Assistants
text:
Many Roles, One Question


Debate

A proposer generates ideas; an adversary attacks them
Disagreement surfaces the weak points early



Ground it

A verifier checks claims against your own library
An analyst builds the data and runs the empirics



Check it

A replicator re-derives the data build and the result, independently
Two paths to the same number, or a red flag




The coauthor skill orchestrates this: you are the coordinator; a debate panel and tool-using subagents do the work in a local folder — no repo, nothing published without you.

title: 7. Personal Assistants
section: Why a Team Beats One Agent
text:
Why a Team Beats One Agent

A single agent that both proposes and checks its own work grades its own homework. Splitting the roles — propose, attack, verify, replicate — is how you catch the beautiful-but-wrong result before it reaches a referee.

title: 7. Personal Assistants
text: Personal Assistants

title: 7. Personal Assistants
section: An Agent That Carries the Work
text:
An Agent That Carries the Work


Give it a goal, not a script

You describe the outcome; it plans the steps
It uses tools — files, code, the web — to act
State persists, so today builds on yesterday



Good first jobs

A weekly digest of new papers in your area
Reformat and check a dataset on arrival
Turn meeting notes into tracked action items




The recurring, rule-ish tasks that eat an hour a week are the sweet spot — worth automating, low cost if a run is imperfect.

title: 7. Personal Assistants
text:
What Makes It an Agent


Not just answering

It decides what to do next, then does it
It checks its own output and retries
It stops and asks when it is stuck



Kept in bounds

You choose which tools it may use
You review before anything irreversible
Give it the reach the task needs — and no more




The skill you are building is not prompting — it is describing the goal well and judging the result. Delegation, not dictation.

title: 7. Personal Assistants
section: Why This Belongs at the End
text:
Why This Belongs at the End

Everything until now was you directing a tool. An agent is you delegating a task — a research team that pressure-tests your work, or an assistant that clears the recurring load. The new skill is knowing what to hand off, and how to check what comes back.

title: 6. AI for Research
text:
The Risk That Matters Most

The biggest academic danger with AI is fabricated references and claims a cited source does not actually support. The better research skills attack this head-on.



Verify every citation
Checked against Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv — bogus DOIs caught before export


Audit every claim
Does the source actually support the sentence? High-severity violations block the output


Flag contamination
Detect citations that may themselves be AI-invented

text: Does It Actually Work?

title: 6. AI for Research
text:
What the Gap Teaches


Extraordinary at the parts

It nails each individual analysis step
Load the data, run the spec, build the table



Not yet trusted end to end

One broken step anywhere fails the whole reproduction
Exactly where human oversight stays essential




The 93/78 split is the honest picture — and the reason you check the chain, not just the links.

title: 6. AI for Research
text:
The Payoff

AI handles the search, the recall, and the first pass — finding the literature, remembering what you read, drafting the prose, refereeing the draft. You decide what matters and whether it is right.

What Else Is in the Plugin



Reference files


One teaching script per module, plus a bank of problems with verified answers
SKILL.md names them but does not contain them — Claude reads a module only when the student gets there

A Python script

The tutoring protocol, the course material, and the arithmetic live in one installable package that any student can add in two commands, and that you can revise once for everyone.

A good skill uses it — filling that template’s own layouts instead of drawing shapes.


What the Skill Adds

Which layout for which kind of content
How much text fits in each placeholder
What to do when nothing fits — a wide chart, a long table




A template guides a person, who sees the result and adjusts. A skill guides Claude, which cannot.

Save and close first
Include in your skill: Save and close any open PowerPoint deck before editing it. Re-open after editing.


Claude cannot see your slides
Claude cannot natively view PowerPoint slides to examine whether things are properly located. It goes PPTX → PDF → PNG.


The route matters

Sometimes multiple skills compete for the same job.


The collision
Anthropic’s pptx skill triggers on any PowerPoint file, so a skill of your own for your desired style will collide with it. Things compound if you create multiple skills for multiple styles.


The fix
Ask Claude to edit your CLAUDE.md to settle the precedence.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Claude

Start with the tool: where these systems came from, what an agent actually is underneath the chat window, and which of the several Claude interfaces is worth your time. The vocabulary matters more than it might seem, because most confusion about what AI can and cannot do traces back to not knowing which piece is doing the work.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
A Brief History



  
    
    2022–2023
    Online chatbots
  
  
    
    2023–2024
    Code and web tools
  
  
    
    2025
    CLI tools
  
  
    
    2025–2026
    CLI in an app
  
  
    
    2026
    Cowork-type agents
  


The arc runs from 2022 and 2023, when these were online chatbots and nothing more — you typed, it typed back. In 2023 and 2024 they gained tools: code execution and web search. In 2025 the serious versions moved to the command line, where the model could read and write files on your own machine. Over 2025 and 2026 that command-line capability was wrapped back into an app, and now, in 2026, we have agents like Cowork that carry out extended work on your files without you living in a terminal.

title: AI/Claude Intro
section: An Agent is a Chatbot with Tools
text:
An Agent is a Chatbot with Tools


Code Execution


↕


User


↔︎


Agent


↔︎


LLM


↕


Other Tools



An agent is a chatbot with tools. You talk to the agent, and the agent talks to the language model. The model itself does nothing but produce text — it cannot open a file or run a calculation. What makes the arrangement powerful is everything hanging off the agent: code execution above, other tools below, whatever has been wired in. The model decides which tool to call, the agent actually calls it, and the result comes back. That separation is the single most useful thing to understand about all of this.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Agent in More Detail






The loop has five steps. You type a prompt. The agent sends the model the system prompt, the tool definitions, and the whole conversation history. The model returns either text or a request to call a tool. If it is a tool call, the agent executes it — running SQL, listing tables, running Python — and sends the result back, looping to step two. Only when the model returns a final answer does anything reach you. The messages array in the middle grows every turn and carries every tool call and result, which is why long sessions get expensive.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Anthropic’s System Prompt
Link to Opus 4.8 system prompt



Every conversation begins with a system prompt you never see, and Anthropic’s is enormous — this one, leaked for Opus 4.8, runs to many pages. It covers tone, refusals, formatting, how to use tools, when to search. Two things are worth taking from it. The behavior you experience is not raw model behavior; it is heavily shaped by instructions. And the same lever is available to you: project instructions are your own system prompt, and they persist across every conversation in that project.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Two Halves of Claude Desktop



Home or Code?
The two halves of the app, chosen at the top of the left sidebar (the square icon toggles the sidebar)











The desktop app splits in two at the top of the left sidebar: Home and Code. The square icon toggles the sidebar if you cannot find it. Home is the conversational side, the descendant of the web chat. Code is the descendant of the command-line tool, built for working directly in a folder of files. Nearly everyone in this workshop wants the Home side, but knowing the split exists explains why the app can look completely different in two people’s screenshots.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Four Modes of Claude Desktop




Within Home, Chat or Cowork?
Toggle in the prompt box













Within Code, Local or Cloud?
Selector at the bottom of the window












Each half splits again, which is where the four modes come from. Inside Home, a toggle in the prompt box chooses Chat or Cowork. Chat is the familiar back-and-forth; Cowork gives the model a working folder and lets it carry out multi-step tasks. Inside Code, a selector at the bottom of the window chooses Local or Cloud — whether the work happens on your machine or on Anthropic’s, against a GitHub repository. Four modes, two toggles, and the toggles sit in different places, which is the genuinely confusing part.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
What to Use?



You can chat in any mode
You can execute code in any mode



Cowork > Chat on many dimensions. Requires paid account.


Code Local is best for most people, but Claude Desktop is not the best venue


Use Cowork for now
(more later)



Code Cloud is GitHub integration, probably overkill


You can chat in any mode and execute code in any mode, so the choice is less consequential than it looks. Cowork beats plain Chat on most dimensions, though it requires a paid account. Code Local is what most people would eventually want, but Claude Desktop is not the best venue for it. Code Cloud is GitHub integration and is almost certainly overkill here. For this workshop, use Cowork — we will come back to the alternatives later.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Configuration

Create New Project + Use a Folder Give Claude access to your local files. Store project-specific instructions.
Auto Automatically approve. Misleading name. Claude decides: safe -> don’t ask permission, possibly risky -> ask permission
Model I recommend Sonnet 5. Capable for anything you probably want to do. Faster and cheaper (easier on token quota).







Three settings are worth changing before you start. Create a new project and point it at a folder — that is what gives Claude access to your local files, and it is also where project-specific instructions live. Set permissions to Auto, which is a misleading name: it does not mean anything goes. Claude judges each action, skipping the prompt for safe ones and still asking about anything possibly risky. And for the model, Sonnet 5 is my recommendation — capable enough for anything in this workshop, and faster and cheaper on your token quota.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Do Not Train


Consumer plans — Free, Pro, Max (what we are on)

Settings > Privacy > Privacy Settings, then turn off Help improve Claude
Direct link: claude.ai/settings/data-privacy-controls
The default on a personal account is on
Off keeps your data 30 days; on keeps it five years



Commercial plans — Claude for Work, Education, API

Your data is never used for training, and there is no setting to find
Includes the API, and the API through Amazon Bedrock and Google Vertex
If Rice moves us onto one of these, the setting disappears from your account — nothing to do




It is one account setting, not an app setting: it covers Chat, Cowork, the command line, and the Academic Studio extension at once. And it is not in the Anthropic developer console — that is a separate product for API keys.


Whether your conversations train the model depends on your plan. On consumer plans — Free, Pro, and the Max plan we are on — the default for a personal account is on, and you turn it off under Settings, Privacy, Privacy Settings, by switching off Help improve Claude. Turning it off also shortens retention from five years to thirty days. On commercial plans — Claude for Work, Education, or the API — your data is never used for training and there is no setting to find. It is an account setting, not an app setting, so it covers Chat, Cowork, the command line, and Academic Studio all at once.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Effective Prompting

Prompting has accumulated more folklore than almost any part of this, and most of it is obsolete. The parts that still matter follow from a single fact: the thing on the other end predicts text. It does not reason about your goals, it does not remember what it told you last week, and it does not push back unless you ask it to. Four consequences are worth building into how you work.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Plan Mode
Claude Desktop has an explicit Plan mode. Or add “plan how to do this before you start.”


Why It Works: Knowledge

Planning pulls relevant knowledge into the context window
The model answers in light of what it just retrieved, not base rates



Why It Works: Scale

Decompose the work into subtasks
Verify each one before the next
Failures stay small and local




Asking for a plan before any work happens is the highest-return habit available. Claude Desktop has an explicit Plan mode, and failing that, just add: plan how to do this before you start. It works for two reasons. Planning pulls relevant knowledge into the context window, so the model answers in light of what it just retrieved rather than falling back on base rates. And it decomposes the work into subtasks you can verify one at a time, which keeps failures small and local instead of discovering at the end that everything is wrong.

title: AI/Claude Intro
section: AI is a Prediction Machine, not a Rational Person
text:
AI is a Prediction Machine, not a Rational Person
Suppose Claude has told you in the past that Method A beats Method B for some task. You ask it to do the task.


Do not assume it will use what it knows. If “A beats B” is not in the context window, and B appeared more often in its training data, it will probably use B.


This is the value of “plan before you act.” Planning surfaces “A beats B,” leading Claude to select A for the task.



To see why planning matters, suppose Claude told you last month that Method A beats Method B for some task, and today you ask it to do the task. Do not assume it will use what it knows. If the sentence A beats B is not in the current context window, and B appeared more often in the training data, it will probably reach for B. Knowledge in the weights is not knowledge in use. Planning is what surfaces A beats B into the conversation, and once it is there, the prediction machine predicts A.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Beware of Tunnel Vision
Prediction also means momentum. Once Claude has started down a path, continuing it is the likeliest next step.


What you will see

It hits a roadblock and tries to get around it
Then another way around, and another — exhaustively, tenaciously
What it rarely does is return to the start and ask whether a different path was the better one all along



What helps

Periodically ask: are there other approaches that might work better for reaching the end goal?
Restate the goal, not just the obstacle — that gives it permission to abandon the path instead of defending it




Prediction also means momentum. Once Claude has started down a path, continuing that path is the likeliest next step, and you will watch it hit a roadblock, find a way around, hit another, and find another way around — exhaustively and tenaciously. What it rarely does is return to the beginning and ask whether a different path was better all along. Two things help. Periodically ask whether other approaches might reach the goal better. And restate the goal rather than the obstacle, which gives it permission to abandon the path instead of defending it.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Steelmanning
Don’t ask AI whether your idea is good. Ask it to make the strongest possible case that your idea is wrong.

Sycophancy: training on human feedback teaches that agreement gets high ratings. Ask “is my plan sound?” and Claude finds reasons it is.
The fix: “What is the strongest argument against this acquisition?”
One step further: have it play a skeptical board member, a regulator, a competitor.


Never ask AI whether your idea is good. Training on human feedback teaches that agreement earns high ratings, so asking is my plan sound reliably produces reasons that it is. That is sycophancy, and it is a property of the training rather than a bug you can prompt away. The fix is to invert the question: ask for the strongest possible case that you are wrong. What is the strongest argument against this acquisition? One step further, have it play a specific skeptic — a board member, a regulator, a competitor — because the role pulls in the objections that role would actually raise.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Numbers Need Code
Never trust AI arithmetic. Have it write and run code.


The Problem

“47.3%” is as plausible as “52.1%” to a next-token predictor
Mental math, rankings, comparisons, aggregations — all unreliable
Wrong numbers stated with complete confidence



The Fix

Ask for Python, and have it run
Arithmetic becomes computation, not prediction
Code execution is built into every chatbot and Claude Code




Never trust AI arithmetic. To a next-token predictor, forty-seven point three percent is exactly as plausible as fifty-two point one. Mental math, rankings, comparisons, and aggregations are all unreliable, and the wrong number arrives with complete confidence. The fix is mechanical: ask for Python and have it actually run. That converts arithmetic from prediction into computation, and it is not an exotic capability — code execution is built into every chatbot and into Claude Code. If a number matters, it should have come out of code you can look at.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
What Not to Do
2022–2023 conventions are now useless or counterproductive.


Skip These

“Think step by step” — reasoning models already do, in hidden tokens
“Take a deep breath” — measurably useless now
“CRITICAL! NEVER EVER…” — overtriggers, and gets worse results



Use With Care

“You are an expert data analyst …”
Persona stacking can improve tone and structure
Direct task framing usually wins




The prompting conventions of 2022 and 2023 are now useless or actively harmful. Skip think step by step — reasoning models already do that, in hidden tokens. Skip take a deep breath, which was measurably useless. And skip shouting: all-caps CRITICAL, NEVER EVER overtriggers and produces worse results, not better ones. Personas deserve more care than outright dismissal. You are an expert data analyst can genuinely improve tone and structure, but stacking personas rarely helps, and direct task framing usually wins.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Code and Documents

Everything the model does beyond producing text, it does by writing code. That one sentence explains the charts, the spreadsheets, and the slide decks, and it also explains the limits on all three. Three examples make the pattern concrete: pulling data from a public source and plotting it, generating a PowerPoint deck from a data request, and building an Excel workbook with live formulas in it.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Example Prompt

Download three FRED (Federal Reserve Economic Data) series as CSV: mortgage rate (MORTGAGE30US), home price (MSPUS), household income (MEHOINUSA672N), 1990 through most recent.

MORTGAGE30US is weekly — resample to quarterly by averaging. MSPUS is already quarterly. MEHOINUSA672N is annual — interpolate linearly between annual observations to produce quarterly values.
Assume a 20% down payment and a 30-year loan. Compute the monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home and express it as a percentage of monthly median household income.
Plot the affordability ratio as a line chart. Annotate three points: the 2006 bubble peak, the 2012 trough (most affordable in decades, as low rates met depressed prices), and the 2023 spike.



The prompt asks for three series from FRED — the thirty-year mortgage rate, the median home price, and real median household income — from 1990 forward. Notice how much of it is specification rather than request. The mortgage rate is weekly and must be averaged to quarterly, the price series is already quarterly, and income is annual and must be interpolated. Then the finance: twenty percent down, a thirty-year loan, and the payment expressed as a percentage of monthly income. Then the chart, with three specific points annotated. That detail is not pedantry — it removes the decisions you did not want it making.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Result






The result is a single line: the monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home as a percentage of median household income, from 1990 through 2024. The 2006 bubble peak reaches about twenty-one percent. The 2012 trough, at fifteen point four, was the most affordable in decades, because low rates met depressed prices at the same moment. And the 2023 spike hits thirty-three point six percent — half again above the housing bubble peak. The whole thing, from data download through annotation, came out of the prompt on the previous slide.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Reading, Editing, and Writing Documents
Claude natively reads text and images, and natively writes text. Everything beyond text is handled by code.

Document reading is doc -> text, then read
Document creation is text (code) -> doc
Office document editing is ‘read and write XML (Extensible Markup Language)’


Claude natively reads text and images, and natively writes text. Everything past that is handled by code, and the pattern is worth memorizing. Reading a document means converting the document to text and then reading the text. Creating a document means writing code that emits the document. And editing an Office document — Word, Excel, PowerPoint — means reading and writing the XML inside it, because those formats are zipped XML underneath. Nothing magic is happening. It is a competent programmer working with file formats.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Example

Get Tesla’s EPS from SEC EDGAR by quarter for the past 5 years. Plot. Create a PowerPoint deck with the plot plus discussion.



The result

tesla.pptx


Three sentences: get Tesla’s quarterly earnings per share from SEC EDGAR for the past five years, plot it, and create a PowerPoint deck with the plot plus discussion. The resulting deck is linked here and you can download it — it is a real PowerPoint file with editable text boxes, not a picture of one. What is worth noticing is the chain: a public data source, a fetch, a computation, a chart, and a document, carried out end to end from a request that took ten seconds to type.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Creating Excel Workbooks
Claude uses Python to create Excel workbooks, inserting numbers (inputs) and formulas cell-by-cell


Example Prompt

Build an Excel workbook containing a mortgage amortization table. Include a chart of the amount going to interest and the amount going to principal each month.



Result

amortization.xlsx


Excel works the same way, with one important difference. Claude uses Python to build the workbook, writing it cell by cell — inputs as numbers, and formulas as actual formulas. Ask for a mortgage amortization table with a chart of the interest and principal portions each month, and what comes back is a live workbook: change the rate and the table recalculates, because the formulas are really in the cells. That matters for teaching, where a static table of numbers and a working model are entirely different objects.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Claude Plugin for Excel
A chat panel inside Excel itself. Add it from Home → Add-ins. You will be prompted to connect to your Anthropic account (paid account).


Example








There is also a chat panel inside Excel itself, added from Home, then Add-ins. It will prompt you to connect to your Anthropic account, and it requires a paid one. The advantage over the desktop app is that it sees the workbook you already have open, so you can ask about the sheet in front of you rather than describing it or uploading a copy. The disadvantage is that it is bounded by Excel — for anything involving outside data or other file formats, the desktop app remains the better place to work.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Verifying Things

The hardest part of working with AI is not getting it to produce something. It is deciding whether what it produced is right, in a situation where you did not do the work and cannot easily retrace it. Five habits cover most of the risk: verifying factual claims, thinking clearly about how code goes wrong, three specific questions worth asking every time, using a second instance as an adversary, and keeping code that already works.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Verify Claims


The Problem

Facts, regulations, dates, citations — stated the same way whether real or invented
The more obscure the fact, the likelier it is fabricated



The Fix

Have it search before answering
Ask for sources. Then check them.




Facts, regulations, dates, and citations are stated exactly the same way whether they are real or invented — there is no tell in the prose, because confidence is not correlated with accuracy. And the risk runs in the wrong direction: the more obscure the fact, the thinner the training data, and the likelier it is fabricated. The fix has two parts. Have it search before answering, which grounds the response in retrieved text rather than recall. Then ask for sources, and actually check them, because sources can be invented too.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Verify Code
Consider a human assistant. Ask where they could have gone wrong.


They may not have understood what you wanted.
To perform the task, they may have had to make decisions that were different from the decisions you would have made.
Their Excel, code, or whatever may have had subtle bugs so it did not do what they expected.


Claude can go wrong in exactly the same ways. How do you check them?

A useful way to think about checking work is to imagine a human assistant and ask where they could have gone wrong. They may not have understood what you wanted. To finish the task they may have had to make decisions, and made them differently than you would have. And their spreadsheet or their code may have had subtle bugs, so it did not even do what they thought it did. Claude goes wrong in exactly those three ways — no more exotic and no less common. The question is how you check for each of them.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Three Checks
Take advantage of the fact that AI is perfectly patient. You can probe more deeply than you would with a human assistant, and it will not be offended.



Check its understanding


Explain to me what you did and how you did it.




Check its decisions


Report all ways in which my instructions were ambiguous and you made decisions we have not discussed.




Check its code


Show me a sample case and work through the case as if by hand so I can verify your number.




Take advantage of the fact that AI is perfectly patient. You can probe far more deeply than you would with a human assistant, and it will not be offended. Check its understanding: explain to me what you did and how you did it. Check its decisions: report all the ways my instructions were ambiguous and you made choices we have not discussed — that one surfaces an astonishing amount. And check its code: show me a sample case and work through it as if by hand, so I can verify the number myself.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Generator-Critic
Spawn a second Claude to attack the first one’s output, not validate it. Subagents work well — several of them.


The Pattern

Generator produces the work
Critic gets: “Find every factual error, logical gap, and unsupported assumption. Do not summarize — find flaws.”



Why a Separate Instance?

A model is anchored to its own output and defends it
A fresh instance with an adversarial mandate is not




A step beyond self-checking is to spawn a second Claude whose job is to attack the first one’s output rather than validate it. Subagents handle this well, and several of them work better than one. The pattern is two roles. The generator produces the work. The critic is told to find every factual error, logical gap, and unsupported assumption — explicitly not to summarize, but to find flaws. The separate instance is the point: a model is anchored to its own output and will defend it, while a fresh instance with an adversarial mandate has nothing to defend.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Re-Use Tested Code
Once code runs correctly, save it. Re-use it rather than rewrite it.


The Problem with Rewriting


Different choices each time
Scripts that should agree may not
Old bugs reappear



Once code runs correctly, save it and re-use it rather than asking for it again. Regenerating looks free, but it is not. You get different choices each time — a different way of handling missing values, a different definition of the same variable — so two scripts that ought to agree quietly do not. And bugs you already found and fixed reappear in the new version, because nothing about the fix was ever written down. A folder of tested scripts is one of the more valuable things you will accumulate.

title: AI/Claude Intro
section: Andrej Karpathy, OpenAI co-founder, former Tesla AI chief, now at Anthropic
text:
Andrej Karpathy, OpenAI co-founder, former Tesla AI chief, now at Anthropic


October 2025
“They just don’t work. They don’t have enough intelligence, they’re not multimodal enough, they can’t do computer use and all this stuff. They don’t have continual learning. You can’t just tell them something and they’ll remember it.”
“I feel like the industry is making too big of a jump and is trying to pretend like this is amazing, and it’s not. It’s slop.”


December 2025
“I really am mostly programming in English now, a bit sheepishly telling the LLM what code to write… in words. Biggest change to my basic coding workflow in ~2 decades.”


February 2026
“It is hard to communicate how much programming has changed due to AI in the last 2 months: not gradually and over time in the ‘progress as usual’ way, but specifically this last December. Coding agents basically didn’t work before December.”
“I don’t think I’ve typed like a line of code probably since December.”



How fast this is moving is easy to underrate, and Andrej Karpathy is a useful witness — OpenAI co-founder, formerly Tesla’s AI chief, now at Anthropic. In October 2025 he said coding agents simply did not work: not intelligent enough, no continual learning, and the industry pretending otherwise was, in his word, slop. By December he was programming mostly in English, calling it the biggest change to his workflow in two decades. By February 2026: coding agents basically did not work before December, and he had not typed a line of code since. Three months, from dismissal to not writing code at all.

text:

The exercise is a business question end to end: merge, filter, aggregate, chart, and produce a deck. After that, two examples about where spreadsheets still belong and where they do not.

title: AI/Claude Intro
section: Merge, Filter, Aggregate, Chart, Analyze, Create
text:
Merge, Filter, Aggregate, Chart, Analyze, Create


Copy this prompt into Claude:

I have five Northwind files in my project folder: customers, orders, order details, products, and categories. Which product categories generated the most revenue from customers in Germany and France? Copy this prompt in as written. It asks which product categories generated the most revenue from customers in Germany and France, showing only categories above ten thousand dollars, sorted highest to lowest, as a bar chart, in a PowerPoint deck with discussion. Every verb in the title is in there: it has to merge five files, filter to two countries, aggregate revenue by category, chart it, and build a document. What would be half an hour of spreadsheet work is one paragraph — and the useful exercise afterward is checking whether the number is right.

Role of Excel
The first spreadsheet program, VisiCalc, was created by a Harvard MBA alum who was inspiried by watching his prof do pro-formas, valuation, and sensitivity analysis on a blackboard with chalk and eraser


Spreadsheets later became the go-to in business for most things numeric


Spreadsheets remain valuable for tabular add-subtract models




Everything else should be done by code written by AI


VisiCalc, the first spreadsheet, was written by a Harvard MBA alum who watched his professor redo pro formas, valuations, and sensitivity analysis on a blackboard with chalk and an eraser, and thought the recalculation ought to be automatic. Spreadsheets went on to become the default tool in business for anything numeric, a far broader role than that origin implies. They remain genuinely good at what they were built for: tabular models that add and subtract. Everything else should be done by code — and now the code can be written by AI.

title: AI/Claude Intro
text:
Takeaways

There is no secret to prompting. Just chat (a lot). Treat AI as an infinitely patient colleague with a poor memory. Code execution gives AI enormous power.


Three things to carry out of the hour. There is no secret to prompting — the phrases people trade around do not matter much, and the way to get good at it is to chat, a lot, and pay attention to what works. Treat AI as an infinitely patient colleague with a poor memory: you can ask anything as many times as you like, and you have to supply the context every time, because it remembers nothing. And code execution is where the power comes from. A model that can run code is a different tool from one that cannot.

Browser and server both on your own computer

A local server often listens on 8000 → visit 127.0.0.1:8000

title: 5. Student Projects
text:
A Chatbot That Can Act


Chatbot

User ↔︎ chatbot ↔︎ model
Each turn sends the user’s prompt, a system prompt, and the history
It produces text — nothing more



Agent

The same loop, plus tools
The model can run code, query a database, call an API
It decides which tool to use, reads the result, and continues

title: 5. Student Projects
text:
What Makes It an Agent


The designer holds every dial


The system prompt — the agent’s role, rules, and refusals
The tools it is given — and, just as important, the ones it is not
The permission mode — what it may do without asking
Limits — how many steps, which actions need a human’s yes



An agent is not a different technology. It is a model, a system prompt, and a carefully chosen set of tools — the anatomy from session one, assembled into something that works on its own.

title: 5. Student Projects
text:
Example: A Database Agent






Ask a business question in plain English; the agent writes SQL, runs it against the database, and answers. The guardrail is built in — it is allowed to read the database but never to change it. Students build this against real data.

title: 5. Student Projects

The pieces

An API key from the Anthropic console, kept in a .env file
The Agent SDK: a few lines to give the model tools and run the loop
Your tools are just Python functions the model may call



The safety dials

Allowed tools and disallowed tools — an explicit list
Permission modes — from “ask me every time” to “run freely”
Start restrictive; loosen only what you trust




The first and best guardrail is a tool the agent simply does not have. If it cannot send email or delete files, no clever prompt can make it.

title: 6. AI for Research
text:
The Research Loop, Assisted


Find

Discover and track the literature
Follow citations forward and back



Organize

A private, searchable library of what you have read
Search by keyword and by meaning



Write & review

Draft and edit with field-aware guidance
Referee your own work before a journal does




Four moves, each with a tool you can install and use today. AI does the search, the recall, and the first pass; the judgment stays yours.

Drafting and Editing


Field-aware help

Structure, argument, and clarity for an economics paper

title: 6. AI for Research

title: 6. AI for Research
text:
Referee Before the Referee


What it produces

A rigorous, source-grounded referee report on a draft
Separate editing notes and a prioritized revision plan
The objections a real reviewer will raise — first



Others have built these too

Pedro Sant’Anna: a full paper-lifecycle suite, adversarial critic-fixer loop
Lee Crawfurd: tightly-scoped review + replication-audit skills
Installable, mostly economists — Claude as copilot, not pilot




The econ-review skill does this for your own drafts. You own the question and the identification; the skill enforces the discipline.

title: 6. AI for Research
text:
The Risk That Matters Most

The biggest academic danger with AI is fabricated references and claims a cited source does not actually support. The better research skills attack this head-on.



Verify every citation
Checked against Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv — bogus DOIs caught before export


Audit every claim
Does the source actually support the sentence? High-severity violations block the output


Flag contamination
Detect citations that may themselves be AI-invented



For empirical or b-school research, this is the line between a demo and something you can responsibly put your name on.

title: 6. AI for Research
text:
Does It Actually Work?


The benchmark

54 social-science papers, tested for whether a coding agent could reproduce the published findings from the paper alone
Claude Code: ~93% at the individual-step level
But only ~78% at the whole-paper level



What the gap teaches

It nails each analysis step
One broken step anywhere still fails the full reproduction
Exactly where human oversight stays essential




The 93/78 split is the honest picture: extraordinary at the parts, not yet trustworthy end to end without a human checking the chain.

title: 6. AI for Research
text:
The Payoff

AI handles the search, the recall, and the first pass — finding the literature, remembering what you read, drafting the prose, refereeing the draft. You decide what matters and whether it is right.
